meta_description: Diálogo is a declarative visual programming environment in which children build games and simulations from symbols they draw themselves. Runs offline on Windows, Mac and Linux, with a sequence of seven activities.
meta_keywords: visual programming, declarative programming, programming for kids, K-12 computing education, drawing-based programming, metaprogramming, block-based alternatives, computational thinking, games without code
og_description: A declarative visual programming environment where children draw their own symbols.
tagline: A visual programming environment where children draw their own symbols
what_p1: It is a programming environment for children over 10 (younger ones with an adult alongside). In Diálogo, programs are built from symbols the children draw themselves. The language rests on two relations between symbols, substitution and categorization, plus about ten combinators (push, pull, teleport, collide, wildcards, an evaluation viewer). With their own drawings and these predefined visual symbols, children build games, simulations and abstract symbolic models, such as numbers and addition from scratch.
what_p2: Rules live on the same board as the game. A character can push a rule out of the way and change the program while it runs, so metaprogramming becomes something a child can see and touch. A step-by-step execution viewer shows which rule fired at each step, and doubles as the debugger.
para_chicos: Build games from your own drawings
Give characters behavior by combining a few visual symbols
See, step by step, why the game does what it does
Make games that rewrite their own rules while you play
para_docentes: Declarative from the first session, with no syntax and no imperative prerequisite
Runs offline on modest hardware, with no account or server; projects are saved locally
Interface in ten languages; adding one more means translating a single text file
A sequence of seven activities delivered as videos addressed to the children, so the tool is easy to adopt

online_note: Or try the online version: it runs the full Diálogo in the browser, with no installation, and can save your files, but it is slow and downloads about 30 MB the first time. For real use, the installed version is much better, and to simply see what Diálogo is about, the introduction by playing is faster.
dev_note: Diálogo is under active development. Bug reports and classroom stories are welcome at agustin@dialog.ar.
step3_p1: Each activity introduces one abstraction mechanism through a playable artifact. Projects 1 to 5 build games; projects 6 and 7 move toward abstract symbolic models. Projects 1 to 3 form a self-contained introduction, with a playable game already in project 2.
step3_p2: The activities are videos addressed directly to the children. The videos are currently in Spanish; an English version is in preparation.

clases.texto: Categorization, the first mechanism of abstraction. Build a board and pieces that capture each other, then replace case-by-case rules with rules over categories.
Substitution, the second mechanism. A growing-body snake, removing duplicated code, and the execution viewer as a debugger.

clases.titulo: Project 3: From Pac-Man to a research submarine
clases.texto: A classic that puts every combinator to work, then re-skinned into a new domain. Simple rules, surprising results.
What happens when a program modifies itself? A labyrinth whose rules can be pushed and pulled during play.
Ideas from game development: event-driven rules, hidden objects, collisions and time control, all combined in one shooter.
Recursion and abstract symbol manipulation. Numbers and addition built from scratch, with no game and no character. It starts out simple and ends up the most demanding of the seven.
Modularity and reuse. Add a scoring system to an earlier game, with no variables at all.
